newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankans look to peace, prosperity.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankans look to peace, prosperity.

text.p: As in many Asian cities, construction cranes tower above Colombo's central business district and workers toil around the clock.
Unlike the case in centres such as Jakarta or Kuala Lumpur, however, the main reason is not a booming economy.

The cranes here are working to rebuild the heart of Colombo, destroyed by a separatist Tamil Tiger bomb in a January attack that killed almost 100 and wounded more than 1,000. RENEWED OPTIMISM AFTER BAD START TO THE YEAR

But after the tragic start to the year, there is renewed optimism among many Sri Lankans about 1997, as government victories regain territory from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and the economy shows signs of an upturn.
President Chandrika Kumaratunga, elected two years ago pledging to end the 13-year ethnic conflict between majority Sinhalese and minority Tamils, says the government has turned the tide in the war.
"I would say that our military strategy has succeeded more than 60 percent, or has succeeded in winning more than 60 percent of the war," she said in a recent magazine interview.

"Our biggest victory is that in the process of military operations, because of the other arm of our strategy... the political one and the devolution (of power)... we have won over the majority of the Tamil people of the north and their hearts and minds."
The Tigers, pledging not to give up their crusade for an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of this Indian Ocean island, dispute Kumaratunga's claim.
The government has offered to devolve power to the regions and has said it would consider allowing foreign mediation in peace negotiations.

There were growing signs during 1996 that international tolerance of the Tigers was waning. For example, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said he would not meet Australian Tamil groups unless they denounced LTTE violence.
But despite the battlefield and diplomatic setbacks, the Tigers remain a lethal force, driven by conviction to their cause and a healthy cashflow from an efficient international fundraising network.
The guerrillas still mount successful raids on government troops and kill senior officers with suicide bombings.
Colombo remains under tight security, its hundreds of military checkpoints and sand-bagged guardposts a constant reminder of the threat of violence.
And Colombo-based diplomats and analysts believe a complete military victory is years away -- if it is ever possible. GOVERNMENT HOPES ECONOMIC GROWTH WILL HELP WIN THE BATTLE
In addition to its military offensive and political reforms, the government is hoping stronger economic growth and improved living standards will deprive the Tigers of potential cadres.
More than 50,000 people have died in the war. The economic cost, too, has been enormous.
Defence spending, the largest single budget outlay, has blown out by 10 billion rupees (US$176 million) in each of the past two years, fuelling the budget deficit.
This hampers the fight against inflation, which is running about 15 to 16 percent, and, in turn, keeping interest rates high.
The once-thriving tourism industry, a major foreign exchange earner, is in deep trouble. Tourist numbers are down about 30 percent in 1996 from 1995, hitting earnings and jobs hard.
Foreign investors have also been wary about Sri Lanka, but there are signs that the Kumaratunga administration's economic reforms are luring back overseas money.
The country has maintained respectable economic growth despite its troubles -- 3.7 percent in 1996 and 5.5 percent in 1995. CENTRAL BANK OPTIMISTIC FOR BETTER 1997

And an optimistic central bank governor A.S. Jayawardena sees things getting even better in 1997, with growth back near the six percent trend, falling inflation and interest rates and increased investment.
Colombo's January bomb blast wrecked the central bank and surrounding buildings. Much of the area remains in ruins.
Speaking in his temporary office in a nearby skyscraper overlooking the gutted shell of his bank, Jayawardena is confident Sri Lanka is entering a new era of peace and prosperity.
"My expectation is that the war will reach some settlement next year," he said. "I am saying this not as a matter of hope but my understanding of the reality.
"You know, everybody is tired of this."
